svg.desc: Banner for a paper on inferring the orbital eccentricities of wide binary stars from one measured angle. Left, schematic: an elliptical orbit seen on the sky, with the brighter star at a focus and its companion on the orbit; a gold line is the projected separation, a blue arrow is the projected relative velocity, and a pink arc marks the angle Gamma between them, which is the only quantity measured. Right: the exact likelihood of Gamma between 0 and 180 degrees for three eccentricities, e = 0.2 (green), 0.6 (blue) and 0.9 (pink), computed from the paper's closed-form formula (Theorem 3.1); each curve is symmetric about 90 degrees and peaks where the absolute cosine of the angle equals e. A dashed gold line at 1 over pi shows the flat angle law of a thermal population with eccentricity density 2e. By Theorem 4.1, different eccentricity distributions never give the same angle distribution. The model assumes random orbital phase and random orientation; no observational data are shown.
svg.text: For wide binary stars, the angle between separation and motion has a closed-form law, and its distribution fixes the eccentricities
Schematic: one binary seen at one moment. Only Γ is measured.
Exact likelihood of the angle for one orbit of eccentricity e
angle Γ · curves computed from the closed form (Theorem 3.1)
Different eccentricity laws never give the same angle law (Theorem 4.1)
